concept: How does heat spread through a metal plate?
title: The Ember Plate
tagline: A flash of heat on cold steel — follow the glow as it fades and spreads.

science.hiddenLaw: Fourier's law of heat conduction: local heat flux q = -k ∇T, so temperature evolves by the heat/diffusion equation ∂T/∂t = α ∇²T with thermal diffusivity α = k/(ρc) — heat diffuses isotropically from hot to cold at a rate proportional to the local temperature gradient.
science.plainStatement: Each tiny patch of metal shares heat with its neighbors, flowing from hotter to colder patches faster when the difference is steeper, so a hot spot fades and spreads out smoothly until the whole plate is the same temperature.
misconceptions: Cold is a substance that flows inward from cold areas, rather than heat flowing outward from hot areas.
Heat only rises or moves upward, so a hot spot would not spread sideways or downward through the plate.
Temperature is conserved or heat spreads like a wave at constant speed, rather than energy being conserved while temperature differences diffuse with spread growing like sqrt(time).
Metal is inherently cold or insulating, so a hot spot would stay localized instead of diffusing through the whole plate.

story.setting: You are in a quiet materials lab with a large, thin sheet of dark steel on an insulated table. An overhead infrared camera shows temperature as glowing color — bright orange-yellow where hot, deep indigo where cold. A precise laser can heat a tiny spot in an instant.
story.mystery: When the laser fires, the bright spot doesn't stay put — but it also doesn't behave like a rising bubble or a frozen dot. Does cold rush in? Does heat only go up? Does the glow keep a sharp edge as it moves?
story.goal: Tune the plate and the laser, watch the thermal glow evolve, and figure out the rule that governs how warmth moves through the metal.

predictions.prompt: You heat a tiny spot in the middle of a cold plate and watch the infrared view. What moves first?
options: Cold flows in from the edges toward the center to cancel the hot spot
Heat flows out from the hot spot to its cooler neighbors, warming them gradually
Both heat and cold stay where they started; the spot just fades in place
Heat teleports instantly to the plate edges, skipping nearby metal

predictions.prompt: If you heat a spot slightly off-center, which way will the warmth spread in the first seconds?
options: Only upward, because heat always rises even in solid metal
Equally in all directions — sideways, up, and down — following the temperature differences
Only along the direction the metal was rolled, not sideways
Nowhere; metal traps heat exactly where it was applied

predictions.prompt: How does the size of the warm patch grow over time?
options: It expands at a steady speed like a ripple, keeping the same sharp edge
It spreads quickly at first then more slowly, with the edge getting blurrier and the peak dropping
It stays the same size while the whole plate instantly jumps to the same temperature
It shrinks back to a point as metal absorbs the heat

predictions.prompt: What happens if you compare a highly conductive plate to one that barely conducts?
options: Both behave the same; metal is naturally cold so heat never moves far
The conductive plate smooths out to uniform temperature; the non-conductive one keeps the hot spot sharp for a long time
The conductive plate keeps the spot sharp; the non-conductive plate spreads heat faster
Heat disappears in both; metal destroys thermal energy

transfer.setup: A single drop of dark ink is gently placed in the center of a still tray of clear water. No stirring, no currents — just still water. An overhead camera records how the color spreads.
transfer.question: What will the ink pattern do over the next minutes?
options: The ink will stay as a sharp dot; water holds it in place
The ink will rise to the top only, not spread sideways
The ink will diffuse outward in all directions, with the darkest center fading and the colored patch growing wider and more blurred
The ink will move outward at constant speed like a wave, keeping a sharp ring

checks.description: With non-zero diffusivity and a hot center on a cold plate, spatial temperature variance decreases over time as heat diffuses.
Peak temperature at the initial hot spot declines as heat flows outward down the gradient.
Mean heat flux magnitude is largest when gradients are steep and declines as the plate approaches uniform temperature, showing flux proportional to gradient.
With insulated (no-loss) boundaries, total thermal energy stays constant while redistribution occurs; mean temperature is flat.
Control: If diffusivity is set to zero, no conduction occurs; variance and peak temperature remain flat despite a large initial gradient.
